title: Water Scarcity: Causes, Effects and Solutions

water that is not salty, for drinking and farming

predictionQuestion: Most of the Earth is covered in water. So why do some places not have enough? What might the lecturer say?

segments.text: Good morning. Our topic today is water scarcity. Water scarcity means that there is not enough fresh water to meet the needs of people and the environment in a particular area. Now, this may seem strange, because most of our planet is covered in water. But as we'll see, very little of that water is fresh and easy to use. Today's lecture has three parts: first, the causes of water scarcity; second, its effects; and third, some possible solutions.

Let's begin with an important distinction. There are two kinds of water scarcity. The first is physical scarcity. This is when there isn't enough water in a region, for example in very dry areas. The second is economic scarcity. In this case, water does exist, but people can't get it, because there are no pipes, pumps or treatment plants, or because they can't afford it. So the problem is not always a lack of water. Sometimes, it is a lack of infrastructure.

Now, what causes water scarcity? I'll mention three main causes. The first is population growth. More people need more water. The second, and perhaps the most important, is agriculture. Farming uses a very large share of the world's fresh water, mainly to irrigate crops. The third cause is climate change, which can make droughts longer and rainfall less predictable.

Turning now to the effects. When water is scarce, people may have to use unsafe water, which can spread disease. Farmers may produce less food. And in many places, someone, often women and girls, must spend hours each day collecting water. This means less time for school or paid work. So, water scarcity affects health, food and education.

So, what can be done? Solutions fall into two broad groups: using water more efficiently, and finding new sources. In terms of efficiency, one key example is drip irrigation. Instead of flooding a whole field, drip irrigation delivers small amounts of water directly to the roots of each plant. Fixing leaking pipes in cities is another simple but effective step.

As for new sources, some dry coastal countries use desalination, which means removing salt from seawater. However, desalination uses a lot of energy and is expensive. Another option is recycling waste water, cleaning it so that it can be used again.

To conclude, then. Water scarcity means not having enough fresh water to meet people's needs. It can be physical, a real lack of water, or economic, a lack of infrastructure or money. The main causes are population growth, agriculture and climate change. It affects health, food and education. And the solutions include using water more efficiently, and finding new sources, such as desalination and recycling.

keyIdeas.text: Water scarcity means not enough fresh water for the needs of people and the environment in an area.
There are two kinds: physical scarcity and economic scarcity.
Economic scarcity: water exists, but there is no infrastructure or people can't afford it.
Three main causes: population growth, agriculture and climate change.
Agriculture is perhaps the most important cause, mainly because of irrigation.
Water scarcity affects health, food and education.
Women and girls often spend hours collecting water, so they have less time for school or work.
Solutions: use water more efficiently, and find new sources.
Drip irrigation delivers water straight to plant roots. Fixing leaking pipes also helps.
Desalination uses a lot of energy and is expensive. Recycling waste water is another option.
